subject: Application - Senior Platform Engineer, GenAI (Amsterdam / Madrid)
paragraphs: I am applying for the Senior Platform Engineer, GenAI role in Amsterdam or Madrid. For the last three years my users have been other engineers: one flake declares thirteen NixOS hosts, an SSH certificate authority, SOPS-encrypted secrets and the task interface they actually type. What made that platform usable was not any single component, but the rule that a change is only real once a gate has read the built artifact back.

The GenAI part of the fleet is the part closest to this role. Models run on one GPU host behind OpenAI-compatible endpoints; MCP servers are wired into the editor from a declared configuration instead of a hand-edited file; multi-agent coding workflows draft changes that shellcheck, deadnix, hermetic builds and document read-backs must pass before they can land. I built an LLM-based knowledge base for consulting work, and I care about the unglamorous half of a shared AI capability: no standing credentials, per-host keys, and evaluation that fails the build rather than the user.

Two things I should be direct about. My daily GitOps is a flake and task gates, not Helm and Argo CD, so I would be learning your delivery stack rather than recognising it; the operating model transfers, the YAML does not. And I live in Germany, so I would relocate to Amsterdam or Madrid. German permanent residence does not transfer, which means a Dutch or Spanish permit is needed, and I would rather plan that openly with your mobility team than discover it at offer stage.

What attracts me to Adyen is that the GenAI platform is judged by whether other teams can ship reliable systems, which is the same test I hold my own fleet to. I would start by making the paved path observable and cheap: a gateway with per-team cost and latency visibility, evaluation as a default rather than a project, and a rollback that is one command. I would welcome the chance to talk through where that would be wrong for your teams.
